label: The Moser Theorems
notes: Welcome to Lecture 7 on printed pages 40 through 43. Today we convert last lecture's homotopy formula into Moser's trick: a single pointwise linear equation whose solution integrates into a diffeomorphism equating two symplectic forms. Stress that this is a flow construction, not a mere classification slogan, and preview the three hypotheses that make it work.

label: Four Notions of Equivalence
notes: Pin down the vocabulary before any proof. Symplectomorphic asks only for some diffeomorphism, strongly isotopic demands an isotopy with a fixed class, isotopic keeps the cohomology class along a path, and deformation equivalent only keeps nondegeneracy. Drawing the implication arrows now stops students from collapsing four distinct words into one fuzzy idea.

label: The Moser Question
notes: State the goal cleanly. Given a smooth path of symplectic forms sharing a cohomology class, we want an isotopy whose pullback freezes the form at time zero. Emphasize that we are not guessing the diffeomorphism directly; we will manufacture its generating vector field and then integrate, which is the entire strategic move of the lecture.

label: Differentiating the Pullback
notes: Walk through the calculation slowly. Write the pullback of omega t under rho t and differentiate in time. The product rule splits into a Lie derivative term and the explicit time derivative of the form. Our target is that this whole expression vanish identically, which converts a global demand into a pointwise algebraic condition we can actually solve.

label: Three Hypotheses, Three Cancellations
notes: This is the heart of the argument, the cancellation ledger. Closedness turns the Lie derivative into d of an interior product via Cartan. Fixed cohomology writes the time derivative as d of a primitive mu t. Nondegeneracy then inverts omega t to solve for the vector field. Each hypothesis retires exactly one term; line them up so the bookkeeping is transparent.

label: The Moser Equation
notes: Highlight the equation that names the lecture. Interior product of v t with omega t equals minus mu t. Because omega t is nondegenerate, the bundle map sending a vector to its contraction is an isomorphism, so v t exists and is unique at every point. This pointwise linear solve is the engine; everything else is integration and bookkeeping.

label: A Two-Dimensional Model
notes: Make it concrete with the notebook's toy path. In two dimensions every form is a density times dx wedge dy, so the Moser equation collapses to one scalar cancellation. The primitive is a quadratic, the vector field points along x, and the residual is machine zero. Encourage students to run the cell and watch the arrows cancel the density's drift.

label: The Nondegeneracy Gate
notes: Show why fixed cohomology alone is not enough. If the density crosses zero the form stops being symplectic and omega t can no longer be inverted, so the Moser equation loses its unique solution. The path must stay inside the open cone of nondegenerate forms. The failure plot is as instructive as the success plot; do not skip it.

label: Moser's Global Theorem
notes: State the payoff theorem for compact manifolds. If two symplectic forms are cohomologous and joined by a path of symplectic forms in that fixed class, they are equivalent by a diffeomorphism isotopic to the identity. Compactness is what guarantees the time-dependent vector field integrates over the whole unit interval, giving a genuine isotopy.

label: The Local Moser Theorem
notes: Present the relative version. Near a compact submanifold where two forms agree, the homotopy formula lets us pick a primitive that vanishes on the submanifold. Then the Moser vector field vanishes there too, so the resulting isotopy fixes the submanifold pointwise. This relative trick is the template for Darboux and the tubular neighborhood theorems coming next.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Consolidate the takeaways. Moser's theorem is a flow construction driven by one linear equation. Fixed cohomology supplies the primitive, nondegeneracy supplies the vector field, compactness supplies global existence, and a vanishing primitive supplies the relative statement. Next lecture deploys exactly this machinery to prove the Darboux theorem and local normal forms.
